opening: “For to me life is Christ, and death is gain.” — Philippians 1:21
body:
When I read Paul's words, I was struck by the extraordinary depth of his devotion. To live is Christ, and to die is gain. Paul knows where his heart belongs. He longs to be with Jesus, yet he recognizes that remaining here means he can continue to serve those who need him.

He is willing to remain where love calls him.

Then, in today's Gospel, Jesus speaks about choosing the lowest place at a banquet rather than seeking a seat of honor.

I found myself wondering why I would want that seat of honor in the first place.

There is something deeply satisfying to me about helping another person. If I had walked a million miles and encountered someone struggling to climb over a rock, I would gladly stop and help them, even if it meant delaying my own journey.

Helping someone forward brings me more joy than arriving first.

Of course, I am not free from jealousy or the desire for things others possess. But when it comes to serving another person, I rarely feel that I am giving something up. I feel that I am receiving something meaningful through the opportunity to help.

Yet a question arose that made me look at humility differently.

What happens when I am the person who cannot get over the rock?

That is much harder.

I am learning to accept help, but it is uncomfortable to feel vulnerable. It is difficult knowing that someone else may have to carry a burden because I cannot carry it alone.

And then I realized something.

When I help another person, I do not necessarily see them as a burden. I see someone I have the opportunity to love.

Why, then, do I assume that someone helping me must experience my needs as a burden?

Perhaps I have been looking at humility too narrowly.

I have thought of it as stepping aside, placing others first, and offering what I can. But humility also means recognizing that I am no less in need of love than anyone else.

If I refuse every helping hand because I cannot bear to be the one receiving, am I truly allowing love to move freely between us?

Jesus does not tell us that our worth depends upon where we sit at the table. And Paul does not measure his life by how much honor he receives. He understands that his life belongs to Christ, and that love gives purpose to whatever place he is called to occupy.

Sometimes that place is beside someone who needs our strength.

Sometimes it is beside someone whose strength we need.

And perhaps the greater humility is learning not to insist upon being either one.

Being the one who always gives is not the point. The point is being wherever love is needed most, whether we are giving it or receiving it.

I want to learn to recognize Christ in both places: in the hand I extend to another and in the hand someone extends to me.

Because love is not diminished when I receive it.

It is allowed to continue.
prayer: Lord Jesus,  Teach me the humility to serve without seeking recognition and the grace to receive without feeling ashamed.  Help me recognize that my worth is not measured by what I can accomplish for others, nor diminished when I need their help.  When someone needs my strength, give me a generous heart. When I need another's strength, give me the courage to accept it.  May I never become so attached to being the one who gives that I fail to recognize Your love when it comes to me through another person.  Lead me to wherever love is needed, and help me welcome it in whatever form it arrives.  Amen.
theme: True humility is being wherever love is needed most—whether we are called to give it or graciously receive it.
title: Give and Take
